questions.question: The Jagannath Temple in Puri depicts which Indian classical dance form?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Odissi.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Odissi** is a classical dance form that originated in the state of** Odisha** in eastern India.
 
• The **Jagannath Temple in Puri **is one of the most famous **pilgrimage sites for Hindus** and is dedicated to **Lord Jagannath, **an incarnation of Lord Vishnu.
 
• The temple is known for its annual **Rath Yatra festival.**
 
• Odissi dance is an** integral part** of the rituals and traditions of the Jagannath Temple.
 
• The temple has a dedicated dance hall called the **Natamandira,** where Odissi performances are held during festivals and other special occasions.
 
• Odissi is characterized by its** graceful movements, intricate footwork, and expressive gestures**.
 
• It is known for its emphasis on the** tribhangi posture**, where the body is bent in three places - the head, torso, and knees.
 
• Odissi has a rich history and has evolved over the centuries, incorporating **elements** from other dance forms and cultural traditions.
 
• It is recognized as **one of the eight classical dance** forms of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kuchipudi** is a classical dance form that originated in the state of **Andhra Pradesh.**

 
 
• It is known for its fast-paced footwork and **dramatic storytelling.**
 
 
 
• **Bharatanatyam** is a classical dance form that originated in the state of **Tamil Nadu**.
 
 
• It is known for its intricate **hand gestures and facial expressions.**
 
 
 
• **Kathak** is a classical dance form that originated in **northern India.**
 
 
• It is known for its fast footwork and **complex rhythmic patterns.**
 
 
 
• While these dance forms are not directly associated with the Jagannath Temple in Puri, they are important part of India's** rich cultural heritage** and have their own unique styles and traditions.

questions.question: Arjuna’s Penance, a mammoth architecture with finely carved rock sculptures, serves as a venue for the Mamallapuram Dance Festival, in the backdrop of the ___________.
questions.solution:

• Stone carvings at the** Pallava historic site depict the Ganges' descent and Arjuna's penance**.

• The relief was made to commemorate **Narasimhavarman I's victory over Chalukya monarch Pulakesin II**.
 
• The area, presently referred to as Mamallapuram, **was formerly known by the nickname Mamallan, the "great wrestler" or "great warrior,"** given to **King Narasimhavarman I of the Pallava Dynasty**.

The correct answer is __**gopuram**__**__.__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Gopuram refers to the ornate and towering gateways that mark the** **entrance** **to the temple grounds in **South India and Sri Lanka**.
 
• Gopurams are typically made of **stone** and feature intricate carvings and sculptures of gods, goddesses, and other mythological figures.
 
• The gopuram's roots are in the early **Pallava kings'** constructions, which are related to North India's central shikhara towers.
 
• There are 21 gopurams (tower gateways) at the **Ranganathaswamy Temple in Srirangam, **Tamil Nadu, which is the tallest temple tower in Asia, the Rajagopuram (shrine of the main gateway), is a striking 239.5 feet (73.0 m) high.

• **Mandap:**

 
 
• It refers to a **pillared outdoor hall **or pavilion used for public gatherings or religious ceremonies.
 
• The mandapa, an **elaborate gateway** that leads to the temple through the gopuram, is a porch-like structure in Hindu temples.
 
• It is a part of the main temple compound and is used for **religious dancing and music**.
 
 
 
• **Ardhmandap:**
 
 
• It refers to a** smaller, semi-open hall** or chamber typically found near the entrance of a temple.
 
• Typically, Ardhamandapa is an open, **four-pillared** structure that stands in front of the temple's mandapa entrance door, allowing for natural light and ventilation.
 
 
 
• **Vimana:**
 
 
• In Hindu temples in** South India and Odisha, East India,** the structure over the garbhagriha, or inner sanctum, is known as the** vimana.**
 
• Vimana refers to the towering, **pyramid-shaped** roof structure that sits atop the sanctum sanctorum (innermost shrine) of a South Indian temple.

questions.question: Which of the following is the style of temple architecture that is widely favoured in northern India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nagar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Nagar** is the style of temple architecture that is predominantly found in northern India.
 
• This architectural style is characterized by its **curvilinear towers** known as Shikhara.
 
• Nagar temples typically have a square sanctum (Garbha Griha) with a central tower.
 
• Examples of Nagar architecture include the **Kandariya Mahadeva Temple** in Khajuraho and the **Sun Temple** in Modhera.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vihar**

 
 
• Vihar refers to Buddhist monastic dwellings, not to temple architecture.
 
• These structures were used as residences for monks and places for meditation and learning.
 
 
 
• **Mandapa**
 
 
• Mandapa is a pillared hall or pavilion in Indian architecture, often used as an entrance to a temple.
 
• It is not a style of temple architecture but an integral part of temple design.
 
 
 
• **Dravid**
 
 
• Dravid or Dravidian architecture is the style of temple architecture that is predominantly found in southern India.
 
• It is characterized by pyramid-shaped towers and intricate carvings.
 
• Examples include the Meenakshi Temple in Madurai and the Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur.
 
 
 
• **Temple Architecture in India**
 
 
• Indian temple architecture is classified into three main styles: Nagara (North Indian), Dravidian (South Indian), and Vesara (a mix of both).
 
• Each style has its distinct features and cultural significance.

questions.question: The architectural marvels, temples of Gangaikonda-Cholapuram, were built by which of the following king?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

questions.question: The part of a temple wherein the main deity of the temple is housed is known as the ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Garbha Griha**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Garbha Griha** is the sanctum sanctorum of a Hindu temple where the main deity is enshrined.
 
• It is typically a small, windowless, and dark chamber located at the center of the temple.
 
• The term **Garbha Griha** literally translates to "womb chamber" in Sanskrit, symbolizing the spiritual core of the temple.
 
• Only priests are allowed to enter the Garbha Griha to perform rituals and offer prayers to the deity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Stupa**: A Buddhist structure containing relics, typically the remains of Buddhist monks or nuns, used as a place of meditation.
 
• **Shikara**: The spire or tower above the Garbha Griha in North Indian temples, symbolizing the mountain peak and representing the divine abode.
 
• **Mandap**: A pillared hall or pavilion in a Hindu temple used for conducting religious rituals and ceremonies.
 
• The **architecture** and layout of Hindu temples are designed to represent the cosmos, with the Garbha Griha being the focal point.
 
• In South Indian temples, the equivalent of a Shikara is known as the **Vimana**.

questions.question: Which of the following temples is NOT an example of Nagara style of architecture?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kailasha temple, Kanchipuram**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Kailasha temple in Kanchipuram is a fine example of Dravidian architecture, not Nagara style.
 
• Dravidian architecture is predominant in the southern part of India, whereas Nagara style is prevalent in the northern regions.
 
• The Kailasha temple, also known as Kanchi Kailasanathar Temple, was built by the Pallava dynasty.
 
• It features a distinct vimana (tower) over the sanctum and intricate carvings typical of Dravidian architecture.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nagara Style of Architecture**

 
 
• Prevalent in the northern part of India.
 
• Characterized by beehive-shaped towers called shikharas.
 
• Examples include Lingaraja Temple (Bhubaneswar), Kandariya Mahadeva Temple (Madhya Pradesh), and Sun Temple (Konark).
 
 
 
• **Dravidian Style of Architecture**
 
 
• Predominantly found in southern India.
 
• Features include massive gopurams (gateway towers) and vimanas.
 
• Examples include the Brihadeeswarar Temple (Thanjavur) and Meenakshi Temple (Madurai).
 
 
 
• **Vesara Style of Architecture**
 
 
• A hybrid style that combines elements of both Nagara and Dravidian architecture.
 
• Found primarily in the Deccan region.
 
• Examples include the temples of the Chalukya and Hoysala dynasties.
 
 
 
• **Pallava Dynasty**
 
 
• Ruled parts of southern India from the 4th to the 9th centuries CE.
 
• Known for their contributions to Dravidian architecture.
 
• Built many rock-cut temples and structural temples, including the Kailasha temple in Kanchipuram.

questions.question: In the South Indian temples, the pyramidal tower is called the ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**vimana**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The term **vimana** refers to the pyramidal tower that rises above the sanctum sanctorum (garbhagriha) in South Indian temples.
 
• It is a prominent architectural feature in **Dravidian-style temples**, widely found in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Kerala.
 
• Unlike the shikhara of North Indian temples, the vimana has a **stepped and gradually tapering structure**.
 
• The vimana often features intricate carvings and sculptures, depicting **mythological stories, deities, and decorative motifs**.
 
• Famous South Indian temples, such as the Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur, showcase some of the most iconic and towering vimanas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dravidian Architecture:**

 
 
• This style is predominant in South India and is characterized by large temple complexes with **gopurams (ornate entrance towers)** and vimanas.
 
• It originated during the rule of the Pallavas (4th–9th century CE) and flourished under the Cholas, Pandyas, and Vijayanagara empires.
 
 
 
• **Sanctum Sanctorum (Garbhagriha):**
 
 
• The innermost and holiest part of the temple, where the principal deity is enshrined.
 
• The vimana is constructed directly above the garbhagriha, symbolizing the **connection between the earthly and divine realms**.
 
 
 
• **Shikhara vs. Vimana:**
 
 
• While the vimana is used in Dravidian architecture, the term shikhara is used for the curvilinear towers in **Nagara-style temples** of North India.
 
• Both structures serve as focal points of temples but differ in shape, style, and symbolism.
 
 
 
• **Brihadeeswarar Temple:**
 
 
• Located in Tamil Nadu, this UNESCO World Heritage site is a prime example of Dravidian architecture.
 
• Its vimana stands at a height of 66 meters and is one of the tallest temple towers in the world.
 
• The temple was built during the reign of Raja Raja Chola I in the 11th century CE.

questions.question: The rock-cut temple of Shiva built by Krishna I is found at which of the following places?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ellora**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The rock-cut temple of Shiva built by Krishna I is the famous **Kailasa Temple at Ellora**, located in Maharashtra, India.
 
• This temple is part of the **Ellora Caves**, a UNESCO World Heritage Site comprising 34 rock-cut monasteries and temples.
 
• The Kailasa Temple is a monolithic structure, meaning it was carved out of a single rock, showcasing **remarkable ancient Indian rock-cut architecture.**
 
• Krishna I, a ruler of the Rashtrakuta dynasty, commissioned this temple in the **8th century CE**.
 
• The temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva and is designed to represent Mount Kailasa, the mythical abode of Shiva.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ellora Caves:**

 
 
• Ellora houses a total of 34 caves, divided into three groups: 12 Buddhist caves, 17 Hindu caves, and 5 Jain caves, symbolizing religious harmony in ancient India.
 
• The caves were excavated between the 6th and 10th centuries CE and exhibit the architectural brilliance of their respective religious traditions.
 
 
 
• **Rashtrakuta Dynasty:**
 
 
• The Rashtrakutas were a powerful dynasty that ruled large parts of the Indian subcontinent between the 6th and 10th centuries CE.
 
• They were known for their patronage of art, architecture, and literature, with the Kailasa Temple being one of their most notable contributions.
 
 
 
• **Kailasa Temple Design:**
 
 
• The temple is designed in the **Dravidian style** of architecture, featuring intricate carvings, sculptures, and depictions of Hindu mythology.
 
• The construction involved removing over 200,000 tons of rock, an engineering feat that continues to awe historians and archaeologists.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO World Heritage Status:**
 
 
• The Ellora Caves were recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 for their exceptional cultural and historical significance.
 
• They attract millions of tourists and researchers every year, making them one of the most iconic heritage sites in India.

questions.question: The Dravidian style of temple architecture can be largely seen from which part of India?

__
 
• The **Dravidian style of temple architecture** is predominantly found in the southern states of India, including Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Kerala.
 
• Prominent examples of Dravidian architecture include **Brihadeeswarar Temple** in Thanjavur, **Meenakshi Temple** in Madurai, and **Ranganathaswamy Temple** in Srirangam.
 
• This style is characterized by **pyramidal towers (Gopurams)**, intricate carvings, and elaborate designs on temple walls and pillars.
 
• The architecture flourished under powerful South Indian dynasties like the **Pallavas, Cholas, Pandyas, and Vijayanagara** rulers.
 
• Key features include **large courtyards, mandapas (pillared halls)**, and water tanks within the temple complex.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dravidian Architecture Features:**

 
 
• Gopurams: Monumental entrance towers that dominate the temple's skyline.
 
• Vimana: The sanctum tower built directly above the sanctum sanctorum.
 
• Carvings: Depictions of deities, mythological stories, and intricate designs.
 
• Use of Granite: Most temples were constructed using durable granite stones.
 
 
 
• **Important Dynasties:**
 
 
• **Pallavas:** Early examples like Kailasanathar Temple in Kanchipuram.
 
• **Cholas:** Known for massive temples like Brihadeeswarar Temple.
 
• **Pandyas:** Contributed to the expansion of temple complexes.
 
• **Vijayanagara Empire:** Famous for temples in Hampi.
 
 
 
• **Significance:**
 
 
• Temples served as cultural and religious centers in South India.
 
• They were integral to social life, facilitating festivals, education, and governance.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO World Heritage Sites:**
 
 
• The Great Living Chola Temples (e.g., Brihadeeswarar Temple) are recognized as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

questions.question: 'Nagara' temples typically have a _______ style of architecture.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **__North Indian.__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **'Nagara' temples typically have a North Indian style of architecture.**
 
• **Nagara or North Indian Temple Style:**
 
 
• Nagara (in North India) is associated with the land between the** Himalayas and Vindhyas.**
 
• The Nagara style is associated with the land between the Himalayas and Vindhyas, the Dravida style with the land between the Krishna and Kaveri rivers, while the Vesara style is sometimes associated with the area between the Vindhyas and the Krishna river.
 
• In North India, it is common for an entire temple to be built on a stone platform with steps leading up to it.
 
• It does not usually have elaborate boundary walls or gateways.
 
• While the earliest temples had just one tower or shikhara, later temples had several.
 
• The **garbhagriha** is always located directly under the tallest tower.
 
• There are many subdivisions of nagara temples depending on the shape of the **shikhara**.
 
• The second major type of architectural form in the nagara order is the **phamsana,** which tends to be broader and shorter than the Latina ones.
 
• Their roofs are composed of several slabs that gently rise to a single point over the centre of the building, unlike the Latina ones which look like sharply rising tall towers.
 
• The third main sub-type of the nagara building is generally called the** valabhi type.**
 
• These are rectangular buildings with a roof that rises into a** vaulted chamber.**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Three main styles of temple architecture are the** Nagara or the Northern style, the Dravida or the Southern style, and the Vesara or Mixed style**. But at the same time, there are also some regional styles.
 
• A number of architectural texts known as the Shilpashastras were written in early medieval times. These refer to three major styles of temple architecture, Nagara, Dravida, and Vesara.
 
• **Dravida Or South Indian Temple Style:**
 
 
• Unlike the nagara temple, the Dravida temple is enclosed by a compound wall.
 
• The front wall has an entrance gateway in its centre, which is known as a gopuram.
 
• The shape of the main temple tower known as vimana in Tamil Nadu is like a stepped pyramid that rises up geometrically rather than the curving shikhara of North India.
 
• It is common to find a large water reservoir, or a temple tank, enclosed within the complex.
 
• Subsidiary shrines are either incorporated within the main temple tower or located as distinct, separate small shrines beside the main temple.
 
• Kanchipuram, Thanjavur or Tanjore, Madurai, and Kumbakonam are the most famous temple towns of Tamil Nadu, where, during the 8th-12th centuries, the role of the temple was not limited to religious matters alone.

• There is an installation of Amalaka or Kalash on Shikhara.
 
• Nagara temples can be divided into many different types according to the shikhara's shape:

• Wagon vaulted buildings and constructions get their name from having a vaulted chamber roof.
 
• Phamsana: These are shorter, but wider constructions made comprised of roofs with multiple slabs that rise up in a gradual slope on a straight incline like a pyramid meeting at one point over the middle of the building.
